questions.title: Fever from infection is caused by resetting the hypothalamic set point
questions.subject: fnd
questions.question: Which of the following pathophysiological mechanisms is fundamentally responsible for the development of a fever during an infection?

options.A: A marked decrease in the basal metabolic rate
options.B: Resetting of the hypothalamic thermoregulatory set point upward
options.C: Complete inactivation of the sweat glands
options.D: Marked dilation of peripheral blood vessels

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fever is associated with an increase, not a decrease, in metabolic rate, as the body actively generates heat to reach the new, higher set point.
explanations.B: Correct. Pyrogens released during infection act on the hypothalamus to reset its thermoregulatory set point upward; because actual core temperature is now below this new target, the hypothalamus drives shivering and vasoconstriction until temperature rises to match it — this is fever. Recognising fever as a regulated shift in the set point, rather than a breakdown of thermoregulation, is the key distinction this question is testing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sweat gland inactivation is not the fundamental mechanism of fever; it can contribute to reduced heat loss during the rising phase, but the driving event is the set point being reset upward.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fever onset is associated with peripheral vasoconstriction, which conserves heat, not vasodilation, which would dissipate it.

questions.learning_objective: Explain fever as pyrogen-mediated resetting of the hypothalamic set point upward, and state that the ensuing shivering and vasoconstriction are the normal response to a body temperature that is now below the new set point.
